rect.title: This diagram is drawn from ply.yaml, the file describing this codebase's architecture and verification claims. Each box is a component; chips are functions with their declared checks; arrows are permitted calls (solid) and data flows (dashed); red bars are forbidden calls. A box's grey depth is how strongly it promises to be checked — white means something inside promises nothing, deeper grey means stronger checks promised, and the weakest function sets the whole box's shade. Hover anything for its meaning. This is a declaration view from `cargo ply render`: it contains no earned evidence, and green is reserved for results from verification.

g.title: ply.yaml — the document this picture is drawn from. This is a declaration view from `cargo ply render`; the verdict strip names whether it contains declarations or evidence. ply: 1 — the format version every rule below is read under; a version this build does not speak is refused, never guessed at

Declaration view from `cargo ply render`. "0 functions promise nothing" counts functions that end up with nothing checked -- whether nobody wrote any checks for them, or the document switched checking off for them on purpose. Run `cargo ply verify` to turn these promises into results; this view reports declarations only.
g.text: Declaration view · 31 components · 62 functions · 0 promise nothing

g.title: This document declares 25 module boundaries inside crates. No check has run in this declaration view, so the boxes and arrows are promises, not results.

component e2e — maps to Rust module ply_e2e Drives the built binary the way a user does, and depends on nothing. A suite that links the library instead stops testing what ships. It had grown exactly that dependency once; the fix was to move the test rather than widen the rule. state VerifyRun — the structure this component holds. The rows below are its fields: each name was found in the code, and each shape read off what that field really is promises nothing as a whole — something inside declares no checks, and one unchecked thing sets the level of everything around it (unclaimed) hollow — promises nothing yet: no functions, no nested components. Saying what it holds is not a promise about how it behaves. Nothing to zoom into; a sketch waiting for claims.

json — one of the things this component holds; the two overlapping outlines mean a structure of your own -- there is more inside it than this row shows. Written in the code as `serde_json::Value`. The name came from the document; the shape and the type came from the code, so this row cannot say something the source does not. The hatching means Ply has no way to make one of these, which is usually why the functions around it come back unchecked.

exit_code — one of the things this component holds; the dashed outline means the value might not be there at all. Written in the code as `Option<i32>`. The name came from the document; the shape and the type came from the code, so this row cannot say something the source does not.

component attrs — maps to Rust module ply_attrs Stands alone. It is a proc-macro crate, compiled for the machine doing the building rather than the machine the program will run on, so a dependency from here into the library would compile perfectly well and would be wrong: the macro would begin depending on the very thing it exists to annotate. promises nothing as a whole — something inside declares no checks, and one unchecked thing sets the level of everything around it (unclaimed) hollow — promises nothing yet: no functions, no nested components. Saying what it holds is not a promise about how it behaves. Nothing to zoom into; a sketch waiting for claims.

component core — maps to Rust module ply_core Everything Ply knows how to do, with no terminal attached. It must never reach up into the command-line layer: that constraint is what makes the engine adapters testable at all, because the moment a diagnostic's wording lives here, the wording and the engine can only be tested together. state Envelope — this document asks to show command, root, diagnostics, coverage, and none of them declare a shape of their own, so none is drawn: a bare name carries no shape, and there is no code here to read one from either linked — 22 components and 56 functions are written down in a different file, `crates/ply-core/ply.yaml`, and drawn here as if they were part of this one. Nothing inside this box is declared in the document you are looking at, so that is the file to open to change any of it. Folding this box away (--depth, --focus, or the viewer's own control) hides them the same way it hides anything else. declares checks up to tested — checked once against the declared examples and generated inputs — the strongest verdict this could earn if every declared check ran and passed; a promise, never a result this box is this shade because `registry.all` is the weakest thing in it: it declares tested — checked once against the declared examples and generated inputs — nothing here is drawn stronger than its weakest part

component cli — maps to Rust module ply_cli state Cli — this document asks to show command, json, and none of them declare a shape of their own, so none is drawn: a bare name carries no shape, and there is no code here to read one from either linked — 3 components and 6 functions are written down in a different file, `crates/ply-cli/ply.yaml`, and drawn here as if they were part of this one. Nothing inside this box is declared in the document you are looking at, so that is the file to open to change any of it. Folding this box away (--depth, --focus, or the viewer's own control) hides them the same way it hides anything else. declares checks up to fuzzed — checked against many random inputs — the strongest verdict this could earn if every declared check ran and passed; a promise, never a result this box is this shade because `join_plainly` is the weakest thing in it: it declares fuzzed — checked against many random inputs — nothing here is drawn stronger than its weakest part

component render — maps to Rust module ply_render Draws a document before any code exists, and writes the same facts as prose. It is the surface a reader judges the whole tool by, which is why its wording is tested by exact string rather than by shape. promises nothing as a whole — something inside declares no checks, and one unchecked thing sets the level of everything around it (unclaimed) hollow — promises nothing yet: no functions, no nested components. Saying what it holds is not a promise about how it behaves. Nothing to zoom into; a sketch waiting for claims.

component check — maps to Rust module ply_check The standalone spec validator, which predates the installed `cargo ply check` command and overlaps it. Retiring one of the two is recorded work, not a decision taken here. promises nothing as a whole — something inside declares no checks, and one unchecked thing sets the level of everything around it (unclaimed) hollow — promises nothing yet: no functions, no nested components. Saying what it holds is not a promise about how it behaves. Nothing to zoom into; a sketch waiting for claims.

cli -> core — cli may call core. That an undeclared cross-component call is forbidden is declared here, and not checked by this build: Ply currently compares crate-level dependencies and does not yet look inside functions, so a call that crosses this line can still go unnoticed (§5.3)

render -> core — render may call core. That an undeclared cross-component call is forbidden is declared here, and not checked by this build: Ply currently compares crate-level dependencies and does not yet look inside functions, so a call that crosses this line can still go unnoticed (§5.3)

FINDING W0419: "check" here means the top-level component `check`, but `core.check` also exists and this name does not reach it. If you meant that one, write `core.check`. check -> core — check may call core. That an undeclared cross-component call is forbidden is declared here, and not checked by this build: Ply currently compares crate-level dependencies and does not yet look inside functions, so a call that crosses this line can still go unnoticed (§5.3)
